title: Agentic Stores (AMS) by 40rty
pitch: Agents arrive with intent, AMS builds the storefront to match. An ask arrives from an assistant, a feed, or a search - AMS serves the storefront to match it over webmcp.
about_excerpt: Agents arrive with intent, AMS builds the storefront to match. An ask arrives from an assistant, a feed, or a search - AMS serves the storefront to match it over webmcp. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every website ever built assumes a human is looking at it. That assumption is baked in so deep we stopped seeing it. Pages exist because humans need somewhere to land. A CMS exists because someone has to author those pages in advance, for every visitor, hoping one of them fits. Agents need none of it. An agent arrives with a specific intent already formed — "wide-fit running shoes under $140 that ship to Tel Aviv by Friday" — then does the absurd work of pulling apart a page built for nobody in particular to find the fraction that answers the question. A hero image it cannot use, a nav bar it will never click, a grid of 48 products to find the four that matter. Everyone is asking how agents should read websites better. The right question is why the website is still a fixed artifact at all. If the visitor states its intent up front, the site does not need to have been written in advance — it can be composed on arrival, from the merchant's catalog and brand system. One agent, one intent, one purpose-built storefront, then it is gone. WebMCP is what makes this possible, because for the first time the visitor tells the site what it came for before the site has to respond. What it does AMS is an agent that streams a storefront over WebMCP. An AI shopping agent arrives at a merchant's store and finds a declared tool surface on navigator.modelContext . It states what the shopper wants. AMS composes a branded storefront for exactly that intent — the right products, the right comparisons, the right attributes surfaced — and streams it back as RFC 6902 patches against a live layout tree. Not a page that was waiting for it. A store that did not exist until it asked. The next turn, the shopper narrows: "actually, only the ones with a wide toe box." The storefront recomposes. Different products, different comparison axis, different layout, same brand. The experience is a conversation, not a destination. The unit of the web stops being the page. It becomes the intent. There is no page to author, no page to maintain and no page to optimize — because there is no page until an agent asks for one. The merchant keeps their brand inside the agentic conversation. Today an agent shopping on a shopper's behalf strips the merchant to a title and a price in someone else's chat window. AMS streams a branded surface into that conversation instead. AMS declares 16 tools through navigator.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool's description and enabled state is overridable per merchant via webmcpConfig , served at session creation — a merchant can rename, re-describe or switch off any tool without a deploy. Tool What the agent gets send_message States an intent in natural language. Hands it to the composing agent and returns its prose. The storefront recomposes as a side effect. show_collection Asks for a named collection or category; the agent resolves it and composes a product layout. get_products Two shapes. Called bare, a compact survey of the canvas — title, price, availability, image. Called with productIds , the full record: description, option axes, and every variant with its exact option values and buyability. get_layout The raw layout tree — component types, props, children. Also the only way to read what was featured , since a look card carries its own product list. get_messages Full conversation history, role-tagged. get_status Session state: isRunning , hasLayout , error, live streaming prose, latest committed reply. get_visitor_context Standing preferences the shopper has stated — size, fit, colour, budget — under the brand's own key names. set_visitor_context States a standing preference. It survives every later recomposition. open_product Navigates the canvas to a product detail view. add_to_cart Adds by product plus {axis: value} selections. Same signal a human card click fires — stamped origin: 'webmcp' . get_cart Every line with its chosen option values, quantity, price, the totals, and whether checkout is available. update_cart_item Sets a line's quantity. Absolute, not a delta. remove_from_cart Removes a line; without selections, every line of that product. begin_checkout Hands off to Shopify's hosted checkout with the current cart. send_signal Escape hatch: a low-level typed interaction signal for anything the typed tools miss. clear_session Resets layout, conversation and session data. Three decisions there are worth naming. Agent-backed tools return the site's own voice, not a status. send_message and show_collection hand the request to the merchant's AI and resolve with its finished text. The operator contract, served to the calling agent at runtime through window.webmcp.instructions , tells it to relay that verbatim: "You operate the tools; the site AI is the voice." The merchant's brand voice survives the round trip instead of being paraphrased by somebody else's model. A turn that outruns the await window returns status: "running" — the caller polls get_status and reads latestResponse . The contract is that the site's voice reaches the agent, not that it arrives within a fixed budget. The cart is addressed by selections, never by variant id. get_products deliberately returns no variant id: those ids are unstable across the optimistic-write window, so an id an external agent held across a turn could aim a write at a line that has already been replaced. Cart verbs take a product plus {axis: value} selections and bind late, against live state — a stale reference can only miss , and fail loudly. This replaced a first version where add_to_cart fell back to "first in-stock variant", so a shopper who asked for size 8 got whatever was in stock first. add_to_cart books itself as a third actor — not the agent, not the visitor, but origin: 'webmcp' . Folding a WebMCP-driven add into either of the others would lie about which surface earned it, and that is the number a merchant asks about first. For agents that do not speak WebMCP natively, appending ?webmcp=1 installs a real host plus a window.webmcp client, so a JS-eval-capable browser agent can call the identical surface. It never overrides a real host — if Chrome or a bridge extension already provided navigator.modelContext , the sim is a no-op. That same flag also makes the URL a self-contained demo: it renders what the page is, and a prompt to paste into an agent. No repo to clone and nothing to send alongside the link. How we built it The storefront is composed, not served. A tool call arrives carrying an intent, and one fixed two-call flow runs: Reasoning — a multi-round tool loop bounded by step count and wall clock. The model fires tool calls as a parallel batch, sees the results and may fire another batch to refine. No prose, no layout. Compose — one streamText call with tools omitted entirely and the reasoning step's tool history flattened to plain text. It streams a jsonl-elements fence that parses line by line into RFC 6902 patch operations against the layout spec. The tool-free compose call is structural, not stylistic. A single tool-bearing call that also composes cannot guarantee output: the model emits a phantom functionCall , finishes with finishReason='tool-calls' and the visitor gets a blank canvas. Strip the tool registry and a phantom call has nothing to execute — the model is forced to compose. It is the most important architectural line in the system. The model split is not the one you would guess. Both calls run Gemini 3.6 Flash by default. The performance split is structural — two calls plus per-step reasoning budgets — not cheap-planner and expensive-composer. Reasoning runs at a minimal thinking floor because a fuller budget measured 13–24s per turn against ~4.6s warm: tried, measured, rejected. Claude Haiku 4.5 and any OpenRouter id are selectable per merchant. The catalog is Shopify's, through Shopify's own MCP. Product search hits the Global Catalog MCP, per-store reads hit the Storefront MCP over JSON-RPC 2.0. Live products, live inventory, live pricing. AMS composes the experience; Shopify stays the system of record, so nothing is mirrored and nothing goes stale. Serving is three planes. Vercel runs the Next.js app that mounts the storefront engine, Railway runs the Hono agent API and Supabase runs Postgres, with Redis holding session state. Streaming is a per-session WebSocket carrying typed events — tool_call , response_text_delta , layout_patch_op , layout_ready , done — so the agent acts on patches while the rest of the surface is still arriving. Entity-id hydration cuts the token bill by roughly 80%. The model never writes product data. It writes entity ids, the catalog declares which props are resolved() and the client resolves them through a HydratorMap . Tokens go to judgment, not to transcribing a product feed.
